audits.title: Controls in fresh meat establishments, meat products establishments and the production of wild game meat

recommendations.text: MISSION DETAILS The mission took place from 6 ­ 10 September 1999. 1.1. Mission team The mission team consisted of 3 veterinary inspectors from the FVO, Unit 1. 2 representatives from the Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia ­ VARS (Central Competent Authority - CCA) accompanied the inspection team throughout the mission. 1.2. Sites visited Two approved slaughterhouses / cutting plants were visited, one of which also had a meat products section (not approved). An unapproved integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment was visited at the request of the Slovenian authorities who adjudged that the establishment was in compliance with EC requirements1. An approved meat products establishment and an approved wild game processing establishment were also visited. An initial meeting and a final meeting took place in the Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia in Ljubljana.

OBJECTIVES OF THE MISSION The scope of the mission was indicated in an official letter from the Director of the FVO to the relevant authorities in Slovenia: the issues to be addressed during the mission were the controls on the production of fresh meat, meat products and game meat for export to the European Community. As part of the above, the team also assessed animal identification and traceability systems as required by Council Directives 72/462/EEC and 96/23/EC. In carrying out its mission, the team focussed on the structure and performance of the veterinary authorities in ensuring that the provisions of Community law are respected in relation to exports of fresh meat, game meat and meat products to the Community. In particular, compliance with the provisions of the following Community legislation was assessed: Council Directive 72/462/EEC (as amended) of 12 December 1972 on health and veterinary inspection problems upon importation of bovine, ovine and caprine animals and swine, fresh meat or meat products from third countries. 1 The Slovenian authorities have commented on this point. No changes have been made to the original text. Page 3 of 16 Council Directive 92/45/EEC of 16 June 1992 on public health and animal health problems relating to the killing of wild game and the placing on the market of wild- game meat. Council Directive 92/118/EEC of 17 December 1992 laying down animal health and public health requirements governing trade in and imports into the Community of products not subject to the said requirements laid down in specific Community rules referred to in Annex A (I) to Directive 89/662/EEC and, as regards pathogens, to Directive 90/425/ EEC. The following additional aspects were also assessed: Requirements relating to the traceability of animals contained in Council Directive 96/23/EC of 29 April 1996 on measures to monitor certain substances and residues thereof in live animals and animal products. Certification of wild game meat (Commission Decision 97/218/EC). Certification of farmed game meat (Commission Decision 97/219/EC).

LEGAL BASIS FOR THE MISSION The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation governing the performance of on-the-spot checks in third countries and in particular: Commission Decision 98/140/EC of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in third countries and Commission Decision 86/474/EEC of 11 September 1986 on the implementation of the on-the-spot inspections to be carried out in respect of the importation of bovine animals and swine and fresh meat from non-member countries Council Decision 95/408/EC of 22 June 1995 on the conditions for drawing up, for an interim period, provisional lists of third country establishments from which Member States are authorised to import certain products of animal origin, fishery products or live bivalve molluscs.

recommendations.text: BACKGROUND This mission was part of a series of missions to Eastern European applicant States provided for in the mission programme of the FVO (DG SANCO) and covering the same issues. Various public health (fresh meat) missions have been carried out in Slovenia in the past, the most recent having been undertaken in 1998 (Document XXIV/1390/98). The report of this mission made recommendations with regard to: · Improvement of the documentation relating to veterinary supervision of establishments. Page 4 of 16 · Definition, improvement and enforcement of the approval procedures for establishments. · Reassessment of the layout, maintenance and cleanliness of meat products establishments. · Improvement in the hygiene of operations and the associated technical equipment. · Improvement of the operation and documentation of establishment own check systems. · Approval of establishment own check systems by the competent authority.

MAIN FINDINGS 5.1. Structure of the Competent Authority The competent authority comprises two component organisations ­ the Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia (VARS) and the Animal Health Centre (AHC). The Central Competent Authority in Slovenia is the (VARS) which forms part of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Food. The structure and responsibilities of the VARS are outlined below. It should be noted that the VARS is not responsible for the provision of day to day supervision in establishments (see section 5.1.2. below)2. 5.1.1. Structure and responsibilities of the VARS The central office of the VARS is based in Ljubljana under the responsibility of the Chief Veterinary Officer. The VARS has 12 regional offices. The central office of the VARS is responsible for the following: · Policy in the veterinary field. · Drafting and proposing legislation in the veterinary field; · Approval of establishments for the Slovenian market; · Proposing (to the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Food) the approval of establishments for export markets (including the EC market); · Control of imports of products of animal origin. This includes the issuing of specific import licenses for such products and direct responsibility for Border Inspection Posts. · Drafting and approval of veterinary export certificates. 2 In their commentary on the draft report, the Slovenian authorities have stressed that the VARS does not have the power to appoint Official Veterinarians. They further state that the Slovenian system for authorisation of Official Veterinarians is contrary to European law ­ this appears to be a misunderstanding of EC law and the mission team made no such assertion. Page 5 of 16 · Scrutiny of and suggestion of amendments to the annual implementation plan of the Animal Health Centre (AHC ­ see below for the structure and responsibilities of the AHC). VARS does not have the power to insist on changes to the AHC plan. Authority for approval of the plan rests with the Minister and the Government. · Organising and delivery of training of VARS staff (a number of workshops are held in conjunction with the AHC). The regional offices of the VARS are responsible for the following · Monitoring of the approval conditions is establishments. This is carried out by regional inspectors of the VARS on a regular basis (monitoring visits in the past were carried out monthly, however this is being amended to an inspection every two months). · The taking of appropriate action where establishments are found not to be in compliance with requirements. Such action may include suspension of export certification, reduction of the rate of production or interruption of the production process until the deficiencies detected are rectified. The regional inspectors of the VARS may propose, to the Minister via the central office, the suspension or revocation of the approval of an establishment. · Initial stages of the establishment approval process (see below). Neither the central nor the regional offices of the VARS have the powers to directly control the implementation of veterinary legislation by the AHC. 5.1.2. Structure and responsibilities of the AHC: The AHC was established as an independent body by the Government of Slovenia. The AHC has a central office based in Ljubljana and is made up of nine organisational units. The AHC is responsible for the day to day delivery of veterinary services throughout Slovenia, including the supervision of the production of fresh meat, game meat and meat products. Other sections of the AHC provide, inter alia, disease control and laboratory diagnostic services. AHC staff have the power to control or stop production. They may also report deficiencies to the regional VARS inspector so that appropriate action may be taken at that level. 5.2. Controls in establishments In relation to controls in establishments, the mission team focused on approval of establishments, veterinary supervision (including traceability and certification of meat and meat products and establishments' own checks), supervision by the regional veterinary authorities and slaughter hygiene. Page 6 of 16 5.2.1. Approval of establishments The system in place until this year may be summarised as follows: · Establishments are required to apply to the local municipality for approval to erect a factory or to modify an existing establishment (this is a general requirement which applies to all types of enterprise and not merely to food producing establishments). The application must be accompanied by detailed plans. · The municipality circulates the plans to the relevant authorities (environment, medical, etc.). In the case of the veterinary authorities, the regional office of the VARS was required to comment on and approve plans ­ conditional approval could be given subject to stated modifications to the plans being made. · Having received the comments of all the authorities consulted, the municipality grants approval for building to commence. The comments received are attached to the approval documentation. Where conditions have been set by any of the authorities consulted these should be incorporated into the plans. · When building is completed, the relevant authorities (including the regional VARS office) are asked to visit the premises and confirm that the building is in compliance with the plans approved, including any modifications stipulated. · At this stage, the operator may apply for temporary approval pending a final decision. · Assuming the building has been deemed to be satisfactory, the regional VARS office informs the central VARS office and national approval is granted. · At this time the operator may apply to the regional AHC for the provision of an inspection service. · Should the operator wish to gain approval for export, he is required to apply to VARS. Following a satisfactory VARS inspection, export approval is proposed to the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Food who may then grant such approval. Earlier in 1999, VARS introduced a revised system for the inspection of establishments prior to approval whereby this is undertaken by a team of three experts appointed from a central list of such persons however this system was not in place in relation to any of the establishments visited during the mission. Page 7 of 16 Implementation of the approval procedure ­ example 13 During an FVO mission to Slovenia in 1998, the mission team found that an integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment (all parts approved for export to EC) and a separate meat products and meat preparations establishment (approved for export of meat products to EC) shared the same approval number (both establishments were owned by the same company). The separate meat products establishment was found not to be in compliance with Community requirements and, as a consequence, the Slovenian authorities were requested to delete the separate meat products establishment and the products section of the integrated establishment from the EC approval list. This was done. Subsequently the Slovenian authorities re-approved, for export to the EC, a section of the detached meat products establishment and assigned a new approval number to this part of the establishment. The products section of the integrated establishment remained unapproved for export to the EC. The procedures for approval of establishments, as outlined above, were not followed in the case and no documentation relating to the process was available. This year the mission team re-visited both the integrated and the detached establishments. In relation to the integrated establishment the mission team was asked to assess the products section to determine whether it could be recommended for approval for export to the EC. In relation to the detached establishment, the mission team was asked to confirm approval for that section to which the Slovenian authorities had granted approval for the export of meat products to the EC. The mission team discovered that the unapproved section of the detached establishment continued to be approved for the Slovenian market with its old approval number which was the same as that used by the integrated establishment for which meat products approval was being sought. Prior to the inspection of the re-approved section of the detached meat products establishment, the mission team was assured by the Slovenian authorities that this section of the establishment had been completely segregated from other, unapproved parts of the establishment and a plan of the establishment was shown to illustrate this. This assurance was found to be false ­ two rooms for storage and weighing/mixing of spices for an unapproved meat products section were discovered within the approved section (the door from the intake area of the approved section to these rooms was not shown on the plan; the mission team were assured, prior to the door being opened, that the door was permanently locked, however, the rooms were in constant use and the only access to them was via the approved section of the establishment); It was also discovered that part of the EC 3 The Slovenian commentary on the draft report states that the establishment was ordered to ensure complete physical separation between the EC approved and non-EC approved sections of the establishment. It is clear from the commentary that approval was subsequently granted without the performance of any verification that this order had been followed. No changes to the text have been made. Page 8 of 16 approved meat products establishment was utilised for the production of raw meat preparations for the local market ­ production of raw meat preparations took place in an area adjacent to the area used for wrapping and packaging of cooked meat products. The mission team also found a new door between the approved section and the unapproved section (where cooked sausages were produced for the local market); raw carton packed meat and cooked sausages were found behind this door proving that it was in regular use and that the EC approved section of the establishment was not adequately separated from the sausage section. The layout of the re-approved section of the detached meat products establishment was not in compliance with EC requirements: there was no logical product flow with many cross-overs of cooked and raw meat and packaged and exposed meat and meat products; routes for evacuation of soiled cardboard were not acceptable. Approval of the meat products section of the integrated slaughter establishment would have led to a situation where it shared an approval number with an unapproved meat products and thus given rise to the potential for fraudulent exports of meat products from the non-approved establishment to the EC. Implementation of the approval procedure ­ example 2 The team also visited an unapproved integrated slaughter, cutting and meat products establishment which was at an advanced stage of the approval process. The Slovenian authorities adjudged the establishment to be in compliance with EC requirements and they wanted to add it to the list of approved export establishments. The construction of the meat products section of this establishment had completed in late 1998. While some of the initial aspects of the approval procedure described above had been followed, the process had not been completed and, in any case, was demonstrably ineffective. Documentation was available which showed that plans had been submitted to the municipality prior to commencement of the project and that these plans had been examined by a regional VARS veterinarian who had approved the plans providing four stipulated alterations were made. Approval for building to commence had been issued by the municipality. Building work had been completed in November 1998 and production commenced at that time however the municipality had not issued a request for an inspection to verify that the establishment had been constructed in accordance with the plans received until mid 1999 and this inspection had not been completed at the time of the FVO visit even though, by that time, the establishment had been in production for approximately 10 months. Documentation was available which showed that the establishment had applied to the regional AHC office for the provision of an inspection service. This request had been complied with by the AHC. Documentation was available which showed that a provisional approval, valid until the end of 1998 had been granted by the VARS. No documentation illustrating the basis on which this decision had been taken was available. Page 9 of 16 No documentation extending this provisional approval was available and the establishment was, therefore, operating in contravention of Slovenian regulations. The plans approved contained many deficiencies in layout with many cross- flows with the potential to cause hygiene problems. One very serious deficiency entailed raw meat being prepared beside the cooker doors. Cooked meat was removed form the cookers by the operatives who handled raw meat. Cooked meat emerging from the cookers comes into close proximity with raw meat. These processes, therefore, constitute a serious public health risk. Only two of the conditions imposed by the regional VARS had been complied with however it appeared that no punitive or remedial action was contemplated by the competent authority. The building had not been constructed in accordance with the plans submitted ­ again it appeared that no punitive or remedial action was contemplated by the competent authority. 5.2.2. Official Veterinary supervision in establishments: The numbers of veterinarians assigned to establishments were satisfactory in all cases. However, as detailed below, the effectiveness of veterinary supervision was unsatisfactory in virtually all establishments visited. On a number of occasions during the mission, the mission team was given information which subsequently was found to be false (e.g. in one establishment the team were told that a locked room was empty when it, in fact, contained ingredients, packaging material and building materials). Training of Official Veterinarians : The VARS has established a training programme for its staff. AHC personnel receive some training from the VARS. The AHC does not have a training programme for the official veterinarians. Documentation containing instructions for the official veterinarians has been issued by the VARS over a number of years. This documentation is quite comprehensive, however, many of the official veterinarians in the establishments appeared to be unaware of the existence of part or all of these instructions. In relation to many of the aspects of supervision detailed below, the official veterinarians did not appear to understand their significance or the underlying principles. Water quality: · Plans of the water distribution systems were not always up-to-date. · All establishments had good systems for the rotation of water sampling points. · In one establishment, the regional AHC laboratory had unilaterally reduced the range of tests carried out on water samples. This problem had not Page 10 of 16 been identified by the official veterinarian or by the regional VARS inspector. Medical certification of workers: · A comprehensive system for medical examination and certification of workers was in place throughout Slovenia. · Checking of the operation of this system (by both the establishment and the official veterinarian) was insufficient in all establishments visited ­ many documents were not signed and/or dated. Scrutiny of establishments'own check programmes: · A major effort was in progress to introduce own check systems in meat product establishments with application of HACCP principles. The legal basis requiring the development of own checks is not yet in place however this is scheduled for September 1999. · In some establishments, the official veterinarian was involved in the development of own check systems, however, the own checks systems were not always comprehensive. · In one establishment it was found that the annual programme of the AHC was not being respected in that the programme specified that 40 bacteriological samples per month should be taken by the official veterinarian and analysed by the official service (AHC). The official veterinarian collected 40 samples per month, however, only 10 of these were analysed by the AHC laboratory ­ the remaining samples were analysed in the establishment's own laboratory. No differentiation was made between establishment results and AHC results and it was therefore not possible for the official veterinarian to verify the accuracy of the establishment sampling programme. Pest control: · Pest control programmes were in place in all establishments, however, these programmes were not sufficiently comprehensive and were not systematically supervised

recommendations.text: Programme of corrective measures A programme of measures should be developed and implemented to rectify the deficiencies detailed in this report. This programme should be comprehensive and detailed. The programme should be submitted to the European Commission. The programme should include the following: (a) Legislative measures The Veterinary Practice Act should be reconstructed. The roles, responsibilities and powers of the veterinary organisations, particularly the official services, should be defined and collated. Other legislation should be amended to eliminate the deficiencies noted in this report. New legislation should be drafted and introduced where necessary. (b) Training A comprehensive syllabus for training of the staff of the VARS should be developed. The syllabus should cover, at least, the following subjects: Ø The responsibilities of the official veterinarian, Ø Slaughter hygiene techniques, Ø Control of health marks and health marked labels, Ø Traceability of meat, Ø Certification, Ø HACCP and the supervision of establishment "own check" programmes and 15 Ø The layout of establishments and the assessment of blueprints. As part of the training programme, a manual for the use of official veterinarians should be developed. This manual should expand and clarify legislative requirements and should detail the supervisory and enforcement tasks necessary to implement the legislation. The TAIEX organisation and the services of the European Commission should be approached for assistance in the delivery of this training. (c) Veterinary supervision in establishments In addition to the operations manual referred to at 7.1.1(b) above, a series of checklists and schedules should be developed to aid the official veterinarians in their work and to harmonise enforcement activities. As a priority, veterinary certification, the supervision of establishment "own checks" programmes and the control of health marks (particularly health marked labels) should be improved. (d) VARS supervision ­ regional and central Criteria and timetables for the inspection of establishments and supervision of official veterinarians by the regional inspectorate should be developed and implemented. The management role of the regional inspectors should be emphasised and enhanced. The "expert commission" should evaluate establishments and the performance of the regional inspectors and local official veterinarians on behalf of the central office of the VARS. This should be done on a regular, structured basis; however, the frequency of such evaluations should not be excessive and should not undermine the relationship between the regional inspectors and the official veterinarians in the establishments. (e) Approval of establishments A protocol should be developed for use by the "expert commission" when approving establishments or assessing their approval status. A programme for re-assessment of all establishments should be put in place. Deficiencies in existing establishments should be identified and deadlines for rectification agreed with the operators of the establishments concerned. (f) Animal identification and movement controls The programme set out in the legislation should be followed. Safeguards and controls should be incorporated in the database structure and functionality. The on-the-spot checks (e.g. on farm, in market, at slaughter) necessary to ensure the effectiveness of the system should be formulated. Additional legislation should be enacted where necessary. 16

Guarantees to the European Commission (a) Interim guarantee Given that the programme requested at 7.1.1 above will require time for its development, and given that Commission Decision 1999/820/EC should be reviewed before 1st February 2000, the Slovenian authorities should provide interim guarantees to the European Commission that it will develop and submit such a programme. This interim guarantee should accompany the response of the Slovenian authorities to this draft report. (b) Programme of measures The Slovenian authorities should submit a programme of measures, as detailed at 7.1.1 above, to the European Commission. The programme should include a timetable for the implementation of the measures concerned. The Slovenian authorities should provide detailed guarantees that the programme will be implemented within the timeframe specified. These guarantees should be provided within 2 months of receipt of the final version of this report. 7.2. To the Commission services It is recommended that the Commission services consider the following actions: 7.2.1. Commission Decision 1999/820/EC Assuming that the guarantee sought at 7.1.2(a) above is received, and in the light of the positive response of the Slovenian authorities to the FVO mission of September 1999, consideration should be given to the revocation of Commission Decision 1999/820/EC. 7.2.2. Review of guarantees received The guarantee requested at 7.1.2(b) above and the associated programme of measures should be evaluated by the Commission services and, if appropriate, amendments sought from the Slovenian authorities. The outcome of the evaluation of the guarantees received should inform decisions on what further action will be required.

Assessment of measures taken by the Slovenian authorities An FVO mission, to evaluate the measures taken by the Slovenian authorities and the effectiveness of such measures, should be included in the mission programme for the latter half of 2000. Addendum: The draft report of this mission was submitted to the Standing Veterinary Committee on 26th January 2000. The recommendations in this report were accepted by the Member States. 17

recommendations.text: Competent Authority The Competent Authority (Veterinary Division) should be given the power to carry out inspections in the fishery products establishments, and should do so in order to be able to certify fishery products intended to be exported.
Legislation The legislation in force in Saint Lucia should be adapted in order to cover all the specific requirements laid down by the Council Directives 91/493/EEC, 92/48/EEC and 80/778/EEC.

Licensed Establishments Considerable structural and functional improvements should be undertaken to upgrade the hygiene of the conditions of production of fishery products in Saint Lucia. In particular, the fishery product establishments which intend to export to EU should meet all requirements of Council Directive 91/493/EEC, including setting and implementation of "own checks" programme (HACCP plan), prior to be approved by the Competent Authority.

Identification Marks For traceability purposes, a system for the identification of the establishment of origin (identification/approval number for the establishment and identification/health mark on fishery products) should be put in place.

Official Controls Inspections of fishery product establishments should be increased, and written evidence of all visits should be routinely recorded by Environmental Health Officers. Regular samples for laboratory analysis should be undertaken on fishery products and potable water within the establishments. In particular, a routine monitoring programme for the presence of chemicals, including biotoxins such as ciguatoxine, histamine (Scombridae, Coryphaenidae, Clupeidae), contaminants present in the aquatic environment (heavy metals, 6 pesticides) and residues of veterinary drugs (aquaculture products) in fishery products should be introduced and implemented. A list of poisonous fish should be drawn up, including specific prohibitions on their marketing.

Laboratories The laboratories should be given the means (staff/equipment/reagents) to perform the tests required by Council Directives 91/493/EEC and 80/778/EEC (quality of water intended for human consumption). A network between the different laboratories (including the realisation of intercalibration tests) should be set up.
Landing Sites Stray animals should be excluded of the landing sites. Ice should be systematically used on board of fishing boats.

Written Assurances Written guarantees should be forwarded to the European Commission in respect of the correction of each of the points listed under each of the topics above. 7.2. For the Commission Services After receiving the satisfactory written assurances sought from the Central Competent Authority, the Commission Services should carry out a further review of the possibility of placing Saint Lucia on List II of Annex to the amended Commission Decision 97/296/EC, including a second inspection mission to St. Lucia. 7

audits.title: Control of residues in live animals and animal products

recommendations.text: To review the drawing up of the Residue Monitoring Plan to ensure that it is in accordance with the requirements of the Directive 96/23/EC;
To ensure that communication between staff is appropriately documented;
To ensure the implementation of quality assurance in laboratories, and in particular to complete the validation of the methods for residues analyses without delay;
Concerning the sampling procedure, to introduce the targeting principle;
Concerning the transport of the samples, to introduce general rules on responsibility transfer;
To improve the security of the intermediate storage of samples, including locking of the devices and records for cooling equipment;
To empower the VARS as soon as possible to carry out checks on distribution and use of veterinary drugs, in order to guarantee adequate supervision;
To enforce surveillance of all levels of distribution of veterinary drugs;

To establish a reliable log-book-system on farms and in veterinary surgeries. The Slovenian competent authority should forward to the European Commission written assurances about rectifying all the points listed above, and provide detailed information on (a) whatever action has been and will be taken and (b) the deadlines by which this action has been or will be completed, within one month after reception of the final report. 8.2. To the Commission Services In the medium term, a follow-up mission should be organised in order to verify the effectiveness of the guarantees and to re-assess the competent authorities, in terms of the control of residues in live animals and products of animal origin. 20 9. audits.title: Fresh meat, meat products and game meat

recommendations.text: To take measures to ensure that the elaboration and implementation of the new rules based on the Veterinary Act is finalised before the end of 2001.
To review wild game meat production in Slovenia, and bring it into compliance with EU requirements.
To improve certification procedures in order to comply with the requirements of Council Directive 96/93/EC.
To improve the approval procedure, and the communication to the Commission services, relating to establishments seeking to export to the EU.
To improve import controls, incoming checks and the system of traceability in order to guarantee the EU eligibility of raw materials.

To ensure that efficient control measures to monitor compliance with EU rules are put in place in establishments and, when necessary, prompt corrective actions are undertaken. The Slovenian competent authority should submit, within three months of receiving the final report, an action plan indicating the action proposed or already taken to address the above recommendations and the conclusions of this report. This plan should include deadlines by which the proposed action will be completed. 9.2. To the Commission Services 9.2.1. To retain Slovenia on the existing lists of countries authorised for the export of fresh meat and meat products, provided that the competent authorities of Slovenia respond in a satisfactory manner within the set deadline to the above recommendations. 9.2.2. To remove the wild game meat establishment from the list of approved establishments until such time as it is considered to comply with EU requirements. 9.2.3. audits.title: Pesticides

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should establish a co-ordinated and comprehensive control plan and associated procedures for all control inspectors involved in the control of the marketing and use of plant protection products, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC. The competent authority should provide the appropriate documentation and training necessary to carry out the controls.
The competent authorities should consider increasing the number of samples of plant protection products being analysed for composition and ensure appropriate follow-up.

The competent authorities should consider clarifying responsibilities regarding the identification, storage and destruction of obsolete pesticides, in order to avoid possible contamination of food, feed and the environment.

The competent authorities should consider increasing the range of pesticides and metabolites in the analytical screens, so as to better reflect those substances being marketed and to ensure adequate enforcement of pesticide MRLs as specified in Council Directives 76/895/EEC, 86/362/EEC and 90/642/EEC, as amended.

The competent authorities should consider increasing the scope of the monitoring programme to broaden the range of commodities of plant origin, particularly fruit and vegetables, and to spread the period of sampling, so as to better reflect dietary intake. In cases of MRL infringements, the competent authorities should put in place systematic, efficient and effective follow-up procedures.
The competent authority should ensure that the provisions of Commission Directives 91/321/EEC and 96/5/EC, as amended, on foodstuffs for infants and young children, are fully implemented.

The competent authorities should consider further improvement in the co- ordination between the Ministries of Health and Agriculture, Forestry and Food in the inspection and sampling for pesticide residues in foods of plant origin. An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. audits.title: Diabrotica virgifera virgifera - Plant Health

recommendations.text: Ensure that for outbreaks after 1 May 2004 in areas, which were previously known to be free from Diabrotica, Commission Decision 2003/766/EC is implemented in full, in particular without exemptions from the requirements for crop rotation or "appropriate treatment" (i.e. treatment against adults);
Not designate any areas mentioned in (1) above as "zones of establishment", as this concept and the associated exemptions from the control measures are not foreseen in the Commission Decision;
Consider to include the western outbreak area and an appropriate area around the front of the eastern invasion in the areas, mentioned in (1) above, for full application of the Commission Decision;

Increase the number of compliance checks on the spot, ideally including all maize farms in the focus and safety zones in the areas mentioned in (1) above, which have been identified in the administrative checks as "potential violators"; these checks should preferably be carried out before the flight period of Diabrotica in order for effective, corrective measures (crop destruction, insecticide treatment against adults) to be put in place;

Increase the chances for early detection in non-infested areas by: - targeting mono-culture maize fields when deploying traps, and - focussing on sex pheromone traps, as they have proven the most suitable at low populations ­ and they are the type specified in the Commission Decision;

Consider a methodical verification of the efficiency of new trap types under Slovenian conditions against the well known types before they are deployed on a wider scale. The Single Authority of Slovenia is requested to submit to the Commission, within two months of receipt of the final report, an action plan addressing the above recommendations including deadlines for their implementation. 15 9. ADDENDUM The Single Authority in Slovenia has with the comments to the draft report (see separate document for the full text) provided a provisional response to the recommendatio s (1), (2) and (3): Slovenia has difficulties accepting especially (1) and (3). They are not considered feasible and Slovenia will not be able to fulfil them. The definition of the area of establishment will be considered. However, much of the conclusions and some recommendations in the report concern areas of continuous spread, for which, Slovenia believes Commission Decision 2003/766/EC currently does not apply. Technical guidance for containment programmes in Community areas where Diabrotica is established is currently discussed at the Standing Committee on Plant Health and would probably be taken into account in the national action plan. Regardi (4): The comments regarding the level of supervision, controls and required sanctions are noted. This area will be comprehensively reviewed and reflected in the national action plan. Regardi s (5) and (6): This will be considered, however, Slovenia is not convinced that "targeting of mono-culture fields when deploying traps" necessarily is the best way of meeting the monitoring requirements of the Decision or of monitoring of the population (flight) pressure from infested areas and therefore believes this should be discussed within a broader expert group. 16

audits.title: Animal Welfare - Transport

recommendations.text: The competent authority should provide sufficient information and instructions for staff, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to carry out official controls at the exit point at the port, including inspections carried out according to Articles 19, 20 and 21 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusions: 14, 15 and 30 Associated findings: 3, 7, 9, 20, 22, 25.

citations.text: Procedures do not indicate that port inspectors should enter data in Traces when a check is undertaken pertaining to part III of a health certificate. The port inspectors do, nevertheless, enter data in Traces according to Article 3(2) of Decision 2004/292/EC for each consignment of animals using the reporting model provided in Commission Regulation (EC) No 599/2004. The data from Traces indicated: 1,925 consignments of cattle were checked in 2017 with 59 consignments (3%) with deficiencies including 24 dead animals in 23 consignments and nine unfit animals in seven consignments. 74 consignments of sheep were checked in 2017 with 18 dead animals in 10 consignments and 16 unfit in five consignments. Records in the port indicated 72 cattle were dead on arrival or euthanised because they were unfit to continue their journey in 2017 and 40 sheep the same; i.e. an additional 39 cattle and 6 sheep above that reported in Traces. The combined total of dead and unfit animals, from the port records, represents 0.09% of cattle and 0.18% of sheep transported by road to the port in 2017. The competent authority had not entered data corresponding to the additional 39 cattle and 6 sheep in Traces, contrary to Article 3(2) of Decision 2004/292/EC which indicates that Member States shall ensure that such data is entered in Traces, i.e. including part III.10 "impact of transport on the animals" which includes fields for numbers of dead and unfit animals. The port inspectors explained that the reason for this under-reporting was that they euthanised unfit animals after they had completed their administrative tasks in Traces and had failed to record these cases. The national contact point for animal welfare during transport stated that all animals arriving at the exit point had been certified by an official veterinarian as fit for transport at the place of departure and therefore only a small number of animals, which get sick or injured during transport, should account for such incidents, and considered it necessary to report all such cases back to the Member State of departure.

All journey logs reviewed by the audit team, some 30 journey logs were reviewed, had deficiencies in the planning for the journey by sea to the non-EU country. The competent authority's checks had not detected this despite, as already mentioned in paragraph 1, their procedures indicating the need for inspectors to take account of the Zuchtvieh ruling and that a transporter needs to be established4. The audit team noted that: 4 In their response to the draft report the authorities argue that a lack of clarity in the provisions of Regulation 1/2005 has led to a lack of clarity in the documentary procedures of the Slovenian competent authorities. They also argue that the mission's finding that none of the journey logs that were examined, irrespective of the country in which they had been filled in, contained an indication of the transporter for transport by vessel is the result of the unclear and tenuous link between the livestock vessel and the transporter in Regulation 1/2005. 6 Port inspectors failed to detect that journey logs did not indicate an authorised transporter responsible for the journey by sea, this should have been indicated in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey log; In all journey logs from one Member State organisers of the transport failed to indicate a transfer to a livestock vessel, although this should be indicated in box 6.1 of section 1 of the journey log. The planning in these journey logs ended at the port; In journey logs from a second Member State, organisers indicated the name of the livestock vessel, and although this indicates that they had considered the journey out of the EU they failed to indicate the name and number of the authorised transporter responsible for this stage of the journey, which should be indicated in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey log.

Procedures emphasise that if animals do not have to rest in the control post, the organisers must ensure that time of arrival at the port should coincide with the start of loading onto the livestock vessel in order to minimise the waiting time inside the port. Journey logs for two consignments, from some 30 reviewed by the audit team, indicated that there had been a delay in unloading animals at the control post, as these two consignments arrived at night and were not unloaded until the following morning, which resulted in journey times being exceeded. The port inspectors indicated that on these occasions, the forwarding agent, who operates in the port to co-ordinate the export, had not notified the port authority which operates the control post of the time the consignments would arrive. There was no evidence that the port inspectors had indicated to the central authority that this issue should be raised with the organisers concerned, who, as highlighted in procedures and as required by Article 5(3)(a) of the Regulation, are legally responsible for coordinating the different parts of the journey. 7

Port inspectors carry out official controls in accordance with Article 21(1)(a),(b) and (c) of the Regulation, and the results of these checks confirm that the majority of animals arrive at the port in good condition, and where necessary, the port inspectors take action to ensure that any unnecessary suffering is dealt with. However, procedures do not indicate that port inspectors should enter all relevant data in Traces after the checks and although port inspectors do enter certain data in Traces they have under-reported the numbers of animals deemed unfit for transport. As a result useful information is not readily available to the authorities in the Member State of departure.

Port inspectors had not detected systematic deficiencies in journey logs and although procedures indicate the relevant legal requirements, they do not instruct inspectors to check critical points such as the planning for a transfer onto a livestock vessel and an identifiable authorised transporter for the journey by sea. The central competent authority was not aware of these deficiencies as it had not supervised the work of inspectors to ensure the quality of controls carried out at exit points. As a result, the competent authorities had not ensured the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, contrary to Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and these deficiencies have not been raised with the authorities of the Member States of departure who have the primary responsibility for verifying journey planning.

Procedures include checklists with sections indicating legal requirements, some of which are additional to those needed for the mandatory controls. For example section 3. of procedures "Performing the checks listed in Section 3 of the Journey log ­ for each journey log" provides requirements for road transport vehicles ("additional provisions for long journeys road transport vehicle"). In practice port inspectors did not perform these additional checks of road vehicles, but did carry out checks, according to Article 21(d) of the Regulation, of the means of transport by which the animals are to continue their journey, i.e. the livestock vessel. The procedures do provide another checklist "requirements for sea transport", but this is a list of legal requirements and there are no instructions for staff, contrary to Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, which would be suitable for making a practical assessment of a livestock vessel.

Procedures emphasise that a transporter, as required by Article 10(1) of the Regulation, needs to be established, or in the case that the applicant is established in a third country is represented in the Member state; however the port inspectors had not identified, for any 10 sailings from this port, any natural or legal person as the authorised transporter for the journey by sea. Procedures do not provide sufficient information or instruction to the port authorities, contrary to Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, how the legal responsibilities for organisers and transporters should be implemented in relation to actors involved in the transport of animals by sea. In practice, the port inspectors make all requests regarding fulfilling the legal requirements for the export of animals to a forwarding agent, or the captain of the livestock vessel, but the competent authority have not defined if either of these actors have any legal responsibilities in relation to the welfare of animals during transport.

The inspection reports of approximately 70 loadings each year, which involve some 18 different vessels, did not indicate any checks of power sources, ventilation or alarms. This is contrary to Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation which requires the authorities to verify before any loading of animals that all the equipment referred to in Chapter IV of Annex I remain in good working order. Procedures did indicate legal requirements for ventilation and alarms but did not indicate how to check these and also, procedures did not indicate the requirements of point 9 of Section 1 of Chapter IV to Annex I of the Regulation, in relation to primary and secondary sources of power.

The competent authority had not provided sufficient information, instructions or access to suitably qualified staff, contrary to Article 4 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to support port inspectors in checking the technical requirements of Section 1, Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, such as air changes per hour on board a livestock vessel. Therefore, the competent authority has not ensured adequate inspections of livestock vessels, as required by the Regulation, and has been repeatedly recommended in previous DG Health and Food Safety audit reports.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that the official controls at the exit point including planning, delivery and reporting of checks carried out according to Articles 19, 20 and 21 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 are effective, as required by Article 4 (2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions: 15, 16 and 31 Associated findings: 9, 11, 23, 29.

citations.text: Procedures emphasise that if animals do not have to rest in the control post, the organisers must ensure that time of arrival at the port should coincide with the start of loading onto the livestock vessel in order to minimise the waiting time inside the port. Journey logs for two consignments, from some 30 reviewed by the audit team, indicated that there had been a delay in unloading animals at the control post, as these two consignments arrived at night and were not unloaded until the following morning, which resulted in journey times being exceeded. The port inspectors indicated that on these occasions, the forwarding agent, who operates in the port to co-ordinate the export, had not notified the port authority which operates the control post of the time the consignments would arrive. There was no evidence that the port inspectors had indicated to the central authority that this issue should be raised with the organisers concerned, who, as highlighted in procedures and as required by Article 5(3)(a) of the Regulation, are legally responsible for coordinating the different parts of the journey. 7

The competent authority had not verified the effectiveness and appropriateness of controls at the exit point; Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the competent authority to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, and the central level were not aware that: Port inspectors were under-reporting the number of unfit animals (see 3 above) and that procedures do not indicate that such checks should be entered into Traces; Port inspectors had not detected the systematic deficiencies in journey logs where organisers had failed to indicate the transfer of animals onto the livestock vessel and to identify a transporter responsible for that part of the journey outside the EU (see 7 above). Procedures do not explicitly instruct inspectors, as part of the checks required by Article 21(2) of the Regulation, to check journey logs and record the result in Section 3 of the journey log. Port inspectors had not raised any issues regarding the failure of certain organisers to plan the journey so that animals could be accommodated in the control post when arriving at night (see 9 above). Procedures indicate organisers' legal responsibilities but apart from indicating the need to minimize the waiting time inside the port, do not indicate how to check and what actions to take in relation to organisers' responsibilities.

Port inspectors had not detected systematic deficiencies in journey logs and although procedures indicate the relevant legal requirements, they do not instruct inspectors to check critical points such as the planning for a transfer onto a livestock vessel and an identifiable authorised transporter for the journey by sea. The central competent authority was not aware of these deficiencies as it had not supervised the work of inspectors to ensure the quality of controls carried out at exit points. As a result, the competent authorities had not ensured the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, contrary to Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and these deficiencies have not been raised with the authorities of the Member States of departure who have the primary responsibility for verifying journey planning.

The authorities' actions, including communications with the Member State of departure, resolved a problem with unweaned calves arriving at the control post which is not equipped to feed these animals. However, the existing procedures were insufficient to enable all relevant levels of the competent authority to be aware of another, albeit less significant problem, where inadequate planning by organisers resulted in animals waiting all night to be unloaded at the control post. As a result, the authorities in the Member State where these organisers operate were not informed of the deficiencies in planning by these organisers.

During the audit, the port inspectors refused the loading of a livestock vessel which arrived, as planned by the organiser, to transport a consignment of 640 pregnant heifers. This livestock vessel had many long standing deficiencies, it was in a generally poor state of repair with many corroded and injurious fittings and lacked several essential systems, but nevertheless it had been allowed to load animals in the Slovenian port in 2017. The port inspectors had not refused any loadings of livestock vessels during the previous four years. The audit team noted that, in its last 10 sailings, this livestock vessel had also loaded animals at the ports of two other Member States. It had a valid certificate of approval issued by the authorities of a fourth Member State.

The competent authority had not verified the effectiveness and appropriateness of controls at the exit point; Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the competent authority to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, and the central level were not aware that: Procedures which list legal requirements for livestock vessels did not provide a sufficient instruction for carrying out a practical assessment of these requirements; Procedures for inspections of livestock vessels did not include the legal requirement for primary and secondary power sources (point 9 of Section 1 of Chapter IV to Annex I of the Regulation); Port inspectors did not carry out the additional checks of requirements for road vehicles listed in the procedures; Port inspectors had not identified an authorised transporter for any journeys by sea, although procedures emphasised that a transporter needs to be established or represented in the Member State. 12 Conclusions on welfare of animals during sea transport

Procedures include the relevant legal requirements but do not provide instructions for inspectors on how to verify these requirements as part of a practical inspection of a livestock vessel. Inspections of livestock vessels are therefore based on the experience of the inspectors, but not all requirements are adequately verified, which could have major implications for animal welfare during sea journeys. The competent authority had not ensured the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, contrary to Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should consider further the risks to animal welfare when the loading or sailing of a livestock vessel cannot take place, so that, in such situations, arrangements can be made to safeguard animal welfare, as required by Articles 22(2) and 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 19 Associated finding: 12, 13.

citations.text: The capacity of the control post is not sufficient to accommodate all the animals loaded onto certain livestock vessels. Co-ordination of the arrival of animals has taken place so that this has not been a problem; i.e. there have been no major delays in transferring animals from road vehicles to livestock vessels. However, the authorities had no arrangements to care for animals where they refused the loading of a livestock vessel and where the number of animals exceeded the capacity of control post. Article 22(2) of the Regulation requires the competent authority to ensure that appropriate arrangements are made to care for animals, and if necessary to unload, accommodate, feed and water them if they are detained for more than two hours. Article 23 of the Regulation also requires the competent authority to be able to take action to safeguard the welfare of animals in situations where it finds non-compliance.

The audit team saw that when the port inspectors refused the loading of a ship (see section 5.5) they had ad hoc discussions with their national contact point, who accompanied the audit team, regarding who to consult and what actions to take and 5 https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/animals/docs/aw_list_of_approved_control_posts.pdf 8 initially they did not have a clear course of action to follow regarding how to deal with consignments in the port and those on their way to the port. The audit team also noted that the transporter responsible for the road transport did not have a contingency plan to put into operation in the event that the authorities refused the loading of animals onto a livestock vessel. Article 11(1)(b)(iv) of the Regulation makes it a prerequisite, in order to be authorised as a transporter they shall have submitted contingency plans for use in the event of emergencies. These should have been provided to the authority in the Member State which granted the transporter his authorisation. Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port

The authorities deal with situations such as their refusal to allow the loading of a livestock vessel on a case by case basis; however, there is a risk that animal welfare may not be safeguarded if there is a delay in a sailing and the capacity of the control post is exceeded as the authorities have not determined any options for the arrangements they are required to make in such situations. 5.5 WELFARE OF ANIMALS DURING SEA TRANSPORT Legal requirements Articles 3, 7(2), 19 and 20 of the Regulation. Findings

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take further measures to ensure that they have access to suitably qualified staff, as required by Article 4(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, when carrying out inspections according to Articles 19 and 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, and approve a classification society to verify the strength calculations of pen rails and decks, as required by Annex I Chapter IV Section I point 1 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 30 and 31 Associated findings: 2, 21, 24 and 28.

citations.text: The central authority has given repeated commitments, first given in 2009, that a system was being devised which included sufficient competence for inspection of livestock vessels. The central authority did give port inspectors opportunities to acquire knowledge and skills, by allowing them to take part in study visits and to take part in drafting the network document on livestock vessels. However, this knowledge was not transferred to create a system which adequately covered the requirements for livestock vessel inspection. 2 Judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union (Fifth Chamber) of 23 April 2015 ­ Case C424/13 see: http://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-424/13 4 5.2 TRANSPORT CONDITIONS ON ARRIVAL AT THE PORT

The competent authority indicated in response to a recommendation in report 2012/6375 and again as part of an action plan for 2015 that they would provide a manual to support inspectors in this task. This has not been provided. The competent authority also failed to deliver on commitments made in response to a recommendation in report 2009/8241, and repeated in report 2012/6375, to set up a system so that the port inspectors would have sufficient professional support for carrying out inspections of livestock vessels. The only evidence of close cooperation between the port inspectors and the Slovenian Maritime Agency was in relation to an incident in 2017 where a livestock vessel loaded with cattle suffered engine failure on leaving the port and had to be towed back to port. However, the port inspectors did not have any professional support for inspecting the "non-veterinary" requirements in Annex I Chapter IV Section 1 of the Regulation for livestock vessels.

The port inspectors concluded that this livestock vessel was deficient regarding points 2(a), 4, 5, 6 and 7 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, i.e.: ventilation, the fresh water system, drainage, lighting, no alarms for these systems and no fire alarms in the decks accommodating animals. However, they had not identified these system failures in their report of their inspection of this vessel in 2017 and admitted that they were not competent to assess some of the "non-veterinary" requirements of the Regulation, such as the number of air exchanges required to provide sufficient ventilation.

In the last five years, the competent authority approved one vessel, according to Article 19 of the Regulation, for the transport of cattle and sheep. Prior to the approval inspection, the forwarding agent submitted certain documents: A declaration from the ship's master that the vessel was a suitable means of transport; A plan of the ship including the animal accommodation, disinfection certificates; A list of crew members; and A list of the last ten ports visited. The competent authority indicated in a checklist that various legal requirements, including those for generators, ventilation and alarms, were compliant. The inspection concluded that the vessel, excluding certain pens and indicating that one deck was only suitable for sheep, met the requirements of the Regulation. The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that they assess ventilation subjectively, based on their experience, and did not verify the air changes per hour required by Annex I Chapter IV, Section 1 point 2(a) of the Regulation. The competent authority has not approved a classification society to verify the strength calculations of pen rails and decks on livestock vessels contrary to Annex I Chapter IV Section I point 1 of the Regulation and this aspect was also not verified.

The competent authority had not provided sufficient information, instructions or access to suitably qualified staff, contrary to Article 4 and 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to support port inspectors in checking the technical requirements of Section 1, Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, such as air changes per hour on board a livestock vessel. Therefore, the competent authority has not ensured adequate inspections of livestock vessels, as required by the Regulation, and has been repeatedly recommended in previous DG Health and Food Safety audit reports.

Procedures include the relevant legal requirements but do not provide instructions for inspectors on how to verify these requirements as part of a practical inspection of a livestock vessel. Inspections of livestock vessels are therefore based on the experience of the inspectors, but not all requirements are adequately verified, which could have major implications for animal welfare during sea journeys. The competent authority had not ensured the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls, contrary to Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: Supervision of the OVs' performance in slaughterhouses falls under the responsibility of the regional offices. There are no procedures on how supervision should be carried out at national level. The arrangements in place and, particularly, the scope, frequency and supervisory methods varies from one region to another. The CA from one region explained that their supervision consists of the inspection of the establishment and of the operator's record keeping. If significant problems are not noted, this is taken to imply that the OVs have performed their duties adequately. This is not in line with Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires the CA to have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls. In another region, supervision directly targets the OVs' performance and official records; for this case the CA explained that there is a coordinator for the slaughterhouses that prepares weekly plans and checks all the slaughterhouses under his/her responsibility on a monthly basis.

Supervisory mechanisms are in place and applied. However, the system is impacted upon by differences in the application between regions, in particular in terms of focus. Moreover, the arrangements applied in one of the two regions interviewed are not adequate to provide assurances about the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls. 5.3 APPROVAL OF ESTABLISHMENTS Legal requirements Article 6(3) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. citations.text: The CCA informed the audit team that they have recently started to collect information about the diagnosis reported in the AMI certificates accompanying the cattle that have been emergency slaughtered. The data shows that: the majority of animals fall into the category "an otherwise healthy animal which has suffered an accident that prevents its transport to the slaughterhouse for welfare reasons" and for a small number of animals the diagnosis was a disease (e.g. pneumonia) and/or specified that the animal could not stand. This situation raises clear doubts about the health status of the emergency slaughtered animal and, therefore, its eligibility for slaughter for human consumption, because the AMI certificates should only be issued for animals declared fit for slaughter, in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624.

Concerning emergency slaughter, the system in place is in general in line with Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. However, for a small number of emergency slaughtered animals the diagnosis reported in the AMI certificates calls into question the reliability of the statements contained in these certificates declaring that the animals are fit for slaughter and therefore eligible for emergency slaughter.

recommendations.text: To ensure that when emergency slaughter is carried out outside the slaughterhouse the persons involved in killing of the animals and in related operations have an appropriate level of competence as required by Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. citations.text: The CCA explained that the veterinarians performing AMI at holdings can carry out the stunning and bleeding of animals. Other people can also perform these activities. This is not in line with Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1009/2009, which requires that killing and related operations shall only be carried out by persons with the appropriate level of competence to do so without causing the animals any avoidable pain, distress or suffering.

citations.text: The Commission auditor noted that, contrary to the requirements laid down in part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, none of the samplers (either in the AFSVSPP regional offices included in the scope of this audit or in the NVI) possessed a mechanical or automatic divider necessary for preparing the final samples in case of the control of constituents, including genetically modified material, or substances likely to be distributed in a non-uniform way in feed materials. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The AFSVSPP brought to the attention of the Commission auditor the observation that part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009 in Slovenian was not fully equivalent to the original version in English.

The Commission auditor interviewed several samplers from the AFSVSPP regional offices and the NVI on the implementation of sampling provisions laid down in Article 1 of, and Annex I to, Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. In addition, a number of sampling records from 2018 and onwards were scrutinised. Based on these, the Commission auditor observed the following: 1) Based on many sampling records seen and one interview, the concept of "sampled portion" was not implemented properly by the samplers. 2) The determination of the analyte's distribution pattern in the matrix was largely properly defined by the samplers. 3) The calculation of the number of incremental samples was largely correct. 4) The legal requirements on the size of the aggregate sample and size/number of final samples were largely properly implemented. 5) Due to the absence of mechanical or automatic dividers (within the respective service), all of the final samples were prepared by quartering, which cannot ensure representative division in case of the control of constituents, including genetically modified material, or substances likely to be distributed non-uniformly in feed materials. citations.text: The audit team examined several approval files and associated records and noted that the approvals granted for the first time to ABP operators followed appropriately the approval steps. However, in two out of the three processing plants visited and operating under the full approval, the audit team noted that even though the operators made significant changes to the processing treatment subsequently to receiving the original approval, the 6 required validation of the altered ABP processing treatment and the validation checks thereof by the plants' operators and the competent authority, respectively, had not been carried out, in particular: a. in one plant, the operator using the processing method 7 for processing Category 3 material has changed the processing equipment, the processing parameters and the system for processing from batch to continuous, and b. in another plant, also applying the method 7 for processing of Category 3 material, the operator has modified the processing machinery by installing a new cooker. The absence of checks by the competent authority on the operator's validation procedures, in case of any significant alterations are made to the processing treatment, such as modifications of the machinery, is not in line with requirements of Section 2(4) in Chapter I of Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The AFSVSPP representatives explained that the above-mentioned deficiencies resulted from some misinterpretation of the approval requirements for already approved and operating plants. The authority undertook to expand the existing approval procedure by including instructions referring to the above situations.

Although the national rules for approval of establishments are in line with EU requirements, they lack clarity with respect to the competent authority actions when significant alterations are made to the process in already approved ABP processing plants. citations.text: In the slaughterhouses visited, official controls on food hygiene covered ABP related requirements in a comprehensive manner. However, the audit team noted that these controls have in certain cases erroneously concluded on compliance with the applicable requirements while in fact the relevant requirements were not met. For example, the official controls have overlooked: a. Improper categorisation of some ABP, namely not-emptied intestines containing digestive track content (thus entirely consisting of Category 2 material) were categorised and collected as Category 3 material and as such dispatched to Category 3 processing plants producing PAP. b. Incorrect filling in of commercial documents, resulting in dispatching ABP without proper description required by of point (6)(f)(ii) of Chapter III of Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, namely on the animal species and the specific reference to the applicable point in Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 for Category 3 material and DP derived from and destined for feeding; and the information on the temperature and intended use, with respect to ABP destined for intra-EU trade.

Official controls in ABP plants are, overall, effective in verifying compliance with most of the ABP requirements, and thus provide a satisfactory level of assurance in terms of the overall compliance of operators. However, controls on food operators from the meat producing sector acting along the ABP chain, although regular, do not pay sufficient attention to operators' obligations concerning the categorisation of ABP and information required in documents accompanying ABP consignments dispatched from meat producing establishments, and as a result, weaken confidence in the overall reliability of these controls and in the safe handling of ABP, and the use of DP.

citations.text: Regarding the BCPs designated by AFSVSPP for food and feed of non-animal origin, the facilities were in general not compliant at the BCP Luka Koper port. At the BCP Ljubljana Brnik airport the facilities for controls on consignments of goods of animal origin were shared with controls of food and feed of non-animal origin. The audit team noted that the unloading and storage facilities for food and feed of non-animal origin at the BCP Luka Koper port did not have adequate drainage and most floors were constructed of tarmac which is not easy to clean and disinfect. This is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted that both BCPs designated by HIRS for controls on food contact materials and food supplements were not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs due to a lack of facilities and equipment. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) and (c) of the OCR and Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In the absence of BCP control facilities, the documentary controls are carried out in regional offices outside the port or airport. The identity and physical checks take place in the storage facilities within the BCP Luka Koper port which do not meet the minimum requirements (see finding 48) or at Ljubljana airport, which also did not have adequate drainage.

Whilst the BCPs Luka Koper and Ljubljana airport were, apart from the housing facilities for animal products to be kept under controlled temperature, compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods of animal origin for which they had been designated, both of them and two of the eight listed control points visited were not compliant with the minimum requirements for the categories of goods of non- animal origin for which they had been designated. This latter shortcoming has the potential to reduce the overall effectiveness of the official control system. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The audit found that there is a comprehensive system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the Union through BCPs in Slovenia which is supported by suitably qualified and experienced staff, documented procedures, information technology systems and good cooperation and communication within and between the competent authorities. The system in place ensures that consignments of animals and goods entering the EU are presented for official controls, and that those controls are, with some exceptions, generally carried out in line with documented procedures and EU requirements. Notwithstanding those generally positive aspects, the BCP facilities and control points did not comply with the applicable minimum requirements for the categories of animals and goods for which they had been designated, reducing the overall effectiveness of the system of official controls. The competent authorities initiated a number of corrective actions during the audit to address the shortcomings found, including the delisting of all control points for goods of non-animal 15 origin. The report includes two recommendations to address the remaining shortcomings identified. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 15 December 2023 with the representatives of the competent authorities during which, the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report.
