recommendations.text: Ensure that competent authorities consistently verify whether all authorised 2. operators comply with all requirements listed by Article 92 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, in particular: 1. consistently verify whether authorised operators possess the necessary knowledge to carry out the examinations concerning the Union quarantine pests or pests subject to measures adopted pursuant to Article 30(1), protected zone quarantine pests and Union regulated non-quarantine pests that could affect the plants, plant products and other objects concerned, and concerning the signs of the presence of those pests, the symptoms caused by them, and the means to prevent the presence and spread of those pests as required by Article 89(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 2. consistently verify whether the results of examinations carried out by authorised operators are recorded and stored for at least three years as required by Article 87(3)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 3. consistently verify whether plant passports are attached by the professional operators to the trade unit of plants, plant products and other objects before they are moved within the Union as required by Article 88 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 4. consistently verify whether authorised operators ensure that appropriate training is provided, when necessary, to their personnel involved in the examinations as required by Article 90(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The recommendation is based on conclusion Nos. 7, 18, 23 and 32. Associated finding Nos. 4, 16,19, 21 and 30. Ensure that non-compliances regarding plants, plant products and other objects required to be moved with plant passports from other Member States are reported via iRASFF as required by Article 95(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and Article 16 of Regulation 2019/1715. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 18. Associated finding No. 16.

citations.text: The ASFVSPP issued detailed procedures for its phytosanitary inspectors regarding the registration of professional operators, their authorisation to issue plant passports, the visual examination of plants, the issuance of plant passports and the official controls on professional operators as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The procedures contain guidance on how to practically implement the requirements, and instructions for official measures in case of non-compliances. Similar procedures for the other CAs are being prepared and expected to be issued at the end of 2024. The own procedures of the other CAs contain limited plant passport related instructions for their staff. Each CA uses checklists to verify if professional operators comply with the requirements listed in Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. However, these procedures contain some differences from the applicable EU requirements. · In line with the ASFVSPP procedures, during official controls inspectors verify that authorised operators have the certificate confirming that they passed the official knowledge test. However, passing the test years before an official control does not mean that the operator still possesses the necessary knowledge and is able to carry out examinations, as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see also finding 16). · The checklists do not contain the obligation of authorised operators to provide appropriate training, when necessary, to their personnel involved in the examinations, as required by Article 90(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Consequently, inspectors did not consistently verify the compliance with this requirement (see also finding 16).

The roles and responsibilities of the different CAs are clearly regulated, with detailed procedures to assist inspectors providing a good basis for the effective implementation of EU legislation. Minor differences in the application of some plant passport requirements mean that Slovenia does not implement all the rules in line with the requirements established by EU legislation.

During the official controls observed by the audit team, the inspectors used checklists to verify whether authorised operators comply with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. These controls were broadly effective. However, the audit team noted the following: · All inspectors verified the content, format and attachment of plant passports issued and received. However, in the case of forest plants for planting the CA tolerates that plant passports are not attached to the commercial units which is a general practice in Slovenia and does not comply with Article 88 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see also finding 30). · Non-compliances regarding plant passports from other MS are not reported via iRASFF contrary to Article 95(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and Article 16 of Regulation 2019/1715. · Inspectors verified the records of examinations of plants carried out by authorised operators. However, a single written statement in their records that examinations were regularly carried out, or records containing that plant health checks were done on particular days without any further details, were also accepted. This way inspectors did not consistently verify whether authorised operators carry out meticulous examinations to show that their plants, plant products and other objects fulfil the EU requirements as required by Article 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. · In line with national procedures, inspectors consistently verified that operators authorised to issue plant passports passed the test organised by the ASFVSPP (see also findings 4 and 14). However, they did not verify if operators are up-to- date and still possess the necessary knowledge to carry out examinations, as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 7 · Inspectors did not consistently verify whether authorised operators provided appropriate training, when necessary, to their personnel involved in the examinations contrary to Article 90(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports

Weaknesses in the annual official controls weaken the level of assurance that authorised operators fully meet the requirements for issuing plant passports. The lack of notification of non-compliances related to plant passports from other MS prevents the implementation of official measures to avoid further occurrence of such non- compliances. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 85 to 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Findings 5.4.1 Examinations by authorised operators

In general, authorised operators visited by the audit team carried out examinations of plants for regulated pests. Based on the records provided to the audit team, the examinations were carried out at appropriate times with regard to the possibility of detecting the presence of relevant pests or signs or symptoms thereof as required by Article 87(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. However, some records did not contain the results of the examinations contrary to Article 87(3)(d) of the same Regulation (see also finding 16). Authorised operators take samples in case of the suspected presence of regulated non-quarantine pests and send them for testing to official laboratories of the CAs. Each authorised operator met by the audit team had defined their critical points and had monitoring records for these points as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.4.2 Examinations by competent authorities including the verification of examinations carried out by authorised operators

The inspectors met were aware of the relevant regulated pests and demonstrated meticulous examinations. The audit team noted that these inspections are done in line with the documented procedures of the CAs at appropriate times with regard to the possibility of detecting the presence of pests, their signs or symptoms. However, verification of the examinations carried out by authorised operators was not consistently done by the inspectors, contrary to Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see also finding 16). 5.4.3 Examinations in relation to the protected zones

The CAs carry out meticulous examinations on plants, plant products and other objects to be moved with plant passports to verify that they fulfil the applicable EU requirements regarding the absence of relevant pests. Authorised operators also carry out the required examinations. However, there are cases when the results of the examinations are not recorded. These examinations are not verifiable, therefore do not provide sufficient guarantees for the issuance of plant passports. 5.5 ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS, INCLUDING RECORD KEEPING Legal requirements Articles 69, 70 and 87 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313 in its entirety Regulation (EU) 2019/827 in its entirety Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety. Findings 5.5.1 Issuance of plant passports by competent authorities

Plant passports are attached to the trade units, replaced or invalidated by the authorised operators. However, in the case of forest plants for planting, the CAs accept that the plant passport is only an accompanying document and is not attached to the trade units. This is not in line with Article 88 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.5.5 Application of the exemptions provided for in EU law

The issuance of plant passports is generally in line with EU requirements. However, accepting that certain plant passports are not attached to trade units is contrary to EU requirements thus compromising the reliability of the system developed for issuing plant passports in Slovenia. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF PLANTS AND PLANT PRODUCTS WITH PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 69, 79 to 83, 88 and 93 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Articles 1 to 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety Findings 5.6.1 Official controls on traceability

citations.text: In 2024, adult P. japonica beetles were captured in traps at two motorway service stations/lorry rest areas along the A1 highway coming from Italy (there are outbreaks of P. japonica in Italy, including one in the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, which borders Slovenia). At the first site (Lukovica), six beetles were found in the same trap over five separate dates in July and August. Following the first detection, a total of eight extra traps were placed at this site in 2024, but there were no findings in any of these additional traps. At the second site (Barje), one beetle was found in a trap on 17 July and one on 5 September. The PHPRMD explained that these service stations are about 8-10 hours drive from the outbreaks in Italy, and that lorry drivers are required to rest for an extended period after 8-10 hours driving, thereby giving any beetles hitchhiking on the lorry an opportunity to fly off the lorry into the surrounding environment.

Slovenia did not establish demarcated areas in response to these findings. The PHPRMD explained that it took this approach because all findings were in traps and visual inspections in a 1km radius showed no evidence of pest damage to host plants. On this basis, it concluded that the pest had not multiplied and that these were isolated findings, so it could avail of the derogation to avoid establishing demarcated areas as permitted under Article 6(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1584. 12

The PHPRMD implements the measures required under Article 6(2) of the same Regulation (i.e. for MS availing of the derogation to establish demarcated areas), with one exception. It immediately intensified the number of traps and the frequency with which the traps were checked in a 1km radius of findings. It also intensified visual examination for the presence of adults and raised public awareness of the pest in the local areas. However, it does not inspect grassland and soil for the presence of larvae as required by Article 6(2)(c). It explained that as no beetles have ever been found outside traps, it sees no scientific reason to meet this requirement. This breach is significant, because it means that the source of the trap findings may be beetles emerging from soil close to the traps, (particularly at the Lukovica site, where all beetles were found in the same trap), rather than hitchhikers. If this is the case, Slovenia would be required to establish demarcated areas in line with Article 5 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1584.

The failure to inspect grassland and soil for the presence of P. japonica larvae in the vicinity of trap findings, means that the CA cannot satisfactorily demonstrate that the source of the trap findings are isolated findings of hitchhikers, rather than beetles emerging from soil (indicating that the pest has established), in which case Slovenia should have established demarcated areas around the trap findings.

recommendations.text: Ensure that simulation exercises are carried out for all priority pests within a reasonable period of time, and with the involvement of all relevant stakeholders, unless Slovenia has recently taken measures for the eradication of the pest as required by Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 78 Associated findings Nos. 75, 76

citations.text: Slovenia does not comply with Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 which requires MS to carry out simulation exercises concerning the implementation of all contingency plans within a reasonable period of time, except in cases where the MS concerned has recently taken measures for the eradication of the pest or pests concerned. Slovenia has undertaken just one formal simulation exercise, a field-based exercise conducted by the FIS and the SFS in 2020 focusing on A. planipennis. The PHPRMD added that it has gained valuable experience through dealing with a suspected case of A. chinensis in 2022 and the trap findings of P. japonica in 2024. The PHPRMD has no schedule of planned simulation exercise but stated that it planned to conduct an exercise by the end of 20252. It explained that in recent years, it had allocated any additional capacity to deal with Grapevine flavescence dorée phytoplasma outbreaks, with the result that it was unable to conduct simulation exercises.

The PHPRMD, in discussions with the audit team, expressed confidence that its planned response to pest outbreaks, as outlined in its contingency plans, means that it is sufficiently prepared for relatively small pest outbreaks. However, it acknowledged that by not conducting simulation exercises, in particular for larger outbreaks, to test the robustness of these plans, there is a risk that it may not be able to access sufficient laboratories, equipment, personnel, external expertise and resources necessary for the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of larger outbreaks of priority pests, as required by Article 25(2)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on contingency plans

The failure to conduct simulation exercises to test the robustness of contingency plans means that the CA cannot demonstrate that it will be able to access the necessary resources to ensure the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of any larger outbreaks of priority pests, if and when these are detected. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The planning and implementation of the comprehensive multi-annual survey programme covering all relevant Union quarantine pests and pests subject to emergency measures gives a solid basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests and provides a reasonable level of assurance that these pests have not established in Slovenia. The planning and 2 In its comments on the draft report in September 2025, the PHPRMD stated that it was dealing with an outbreak of P. japonica. 18 implementation of the annual survey programmes for priority pests provides a sufficient level of confidence that any outbreaks of these pests will be detected promptly. Slovenia has published all required contingency plans for priority pests and updates these plans as required. However, simulation exercises to test the robustness of these plans have not been conducted. Consequently, the CA may not be sufficiently prepared to ensure the rapid and effective eradication or, where appropriate, containment of any larger outbreaks of priority pests, if and when these are detected. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting between the audit team and representatives of the AFSVSPP was held in Ljubljana on 20 June 2025, during which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit team were presented. The NPPO offered initial comments on the findings and conclusions presented by the audit team. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The Commission invites the competent authorities to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion (`action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below. citations.text: In the same year, one out of the two registered manufacturers and one out of the two registered re-packers were inspected. The audit team witnessed an inspection of a manufacturer and noted that phytosanitary inspectors reviewed the records of PPP production, raw materials, sales as well as disposal of obsolete, expired or out of specifications PPPs, and also inspected the warehouses. recommendations.text: To put in place appropriate methods or techniques, according to article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in order to verify that the sale of PPPs authorised for professional use are restricted to individuals holding a training certificate, as laid down by Article 6(2) of Directive 2009/128/EC. citations.text: The retailer visited during the audit was aware that PPPs for professional use are to be sold only to those holding a valid training certificate. However, the sales records he kept and made available to the inspectors did not include buyer details. Thus, it cannot be verified that all sales of PPPs for professional use are restricted to eligible buyers, which is not in line with Article 6(2) of Directive 2009/128/EC. The CA confirmed that keeping records without reference to buyers is in line with national requirements and mentioned that, in the past, inspectors may have secretly posed as buyers to monitor compliance with this obligation.

There are no methods or techniques to verify that sales of PPPs authorised for professional use only are restricted to persons holding a valid training certificate . 5.3.2.
